title: Don't call the scriptures false
hookLine: don't call the Vedas and the Semitic books false; false is the one who doesn't reflect (Prabhati, Kabir, ang 1350)
tomorrow: I am the worst of all

lines: A LINE IN A DIFFERENT PLACE.
cards: Two shelves. On one, the Vedas, the old hymns of the Hindu tradition. On the other, the Kateb, Kabir's word for the books of the Muslim neighbors, the Qur'an among them.

A weaver who has just told a learned man that birth makes no one higher might be expected to sweep both shelves onto the floor. If caste doesn't count, maybe the books don't either. That's not what he does.
In Raag Prabhati, Kabir draws a line in a very different place.

teach.h: FROM ONE LIGHT, THE WHOLE CREATION.
teach.b: Kabir's hymns in Raag Prabhati sit close together on the page. One opens wide: first, God made the light, and from that one light the whole creation came. So who is good and who is bad?
Then, in a neighboring hymn, comes the line in today's title. Don't say the Vedas and the Kateb are false.

teach.h: FALSE IS THE ONE WHO DOESN'T REFLECT.
teach.b: False is the one who doesn't reflect. That moves the problem.

teach.h: THE DANGER SITS IN THE READER.
teach.b: The danger isn't sitting on the shelf. It's sitting in the reader. A book can be read with care or with no thought at all; someone can carry a holy text everywhere and never once stop to think about what it asks.
Kabir points there, not at the pages. And he isn't saying all books say the same thing, or asking anyone to give up their own.
He's naming a habit: dismissing a scripture you haven't sat with, or reciting your own without letting it reach you. Both skip the same step.
The word in the line is bichar: to reflect, to think something through.
Sikh teachers say the Guru's word asks to be understood, not only recited.
Read that way, Kabir's line asks the same of every reader, whatever shelf they read from: sit with a line before calling a book empty, and let your own book reach you before calling it full.

how: Sikhs sing this Prabhati hymn of Kabir in kirtan, and Sikh teachers use its line on the Vedas and the Kateb to call listeners to reflect on scripture rather than dismiss anyone's.

o: to argue a book is false or empty
to recite a holy text from memory
to reflect, to think something through

games.q: don't call the scriptures false — tap the pairs.
p: the old hymns of the Hindu tradition
to reflect, to think it through

s: Kabir tells his listeners to throw out the Vedas and the Kateb
he says don't call them false; false is the one who doesn't reflect.
a Prabhati hymn of Kabir says creation came from one light
God made the light, and from that one light the whole creation came.
Kabir says all books say exactly the same thing
he doesn't. he names a habit: dismissing without reflecting.

games.q: you're Kabir. you've just told a proud man that birth makes no one higher. now someone asks: so are the holy books false too? what do you say?
o: don't call them false; false is the one who doesn't reflect.
only my own book is true.
games.why: Kabir moves the problem from the page to the reader: the false one is whoever doesn't reflect.

practice: Bring one line of any scripture to mind, your own, a neighbor's, one you've only heard quoted, or today's: false is the one who doesn't reflect.
Say it slowly inside and ask what it is asking of you, without arguing and without rushing to agree, turning it like a stone in your hand. If you pray, you can say Waheguru before and after.

wordCard.voice: Bichar. To reflect, to think something through: Kabir's word for the one thing a reader of any scripture owes it before calling it empty.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: reflection, thinking something through. Kabir's line turns on it.

carryVoice: Your line: reflect, don't dismiss. The danger sits in the reader, not on the shelf. Day seven hundred fifty-three, done.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Raag Prabhati, Kabir, Ang 1349–1350 (from one light, all creation; 'don't say the Vedas and the Kateb are false; false is the one who doesn't reflect')
